long_form:
идти/ходить and ехать/ездить encode a directionality distinction baked in before any prefix is added and before any question of completion arises: Russian forces a choice between "one trip, one direction, happening now or at one specific narrated moment" (идти, ехать) and "habitual, repeated, back-and-forth, or a completed round trip" (ходить, ездить), even in the most basic present-tense sentence.

This is an older, narrower layer of the verb system than the sweeping imperfective/perfective opposition that organizes everything else — motion verbs preserve what looks like a remnant of a richer Proto-Indo-European set of directional and manner-of-action distinctions that got leveled out almost everywhere else in the verb system but survived, unusually robustly, in this one semantic domain across the whole Slavic family, each language keeping its own version of the same underlying split.

English simply doesn't grammaticalize this at all. "I'm going to the movies" works identically whether it's a specific trip happening right now or a general habit — English adds an adverb ("every week") to signal habituality, but the verb itself never changes shape. That means an English speaker isn't just learning a new ending here, they're learning to notice an entire semantic dimension their own language never requires them to track.

The signature error is reaching for идти/ехать (the unidirectional member) for habitual or repeated motion, simply because English "I go" translates most directly and unreflectively onto идти's dictionary-citation feel. The reverse error — using ходить/ездить for a single trip in progress right now — happens too, but far less often, since it requires overriding rather than following the natural translation instinct.

One of the trickiest applications doesn't fit neatly into either "habitual" or "in progress": the round-trip past-tense use of the multidirectional verb, as in Вчера мы ходили в кино ("we went to the movies yesterday"), which implies the whole excursion — going and coming back — is being reported as one completed episode. That's a genuine third use, distinct from repetition, and it tends to become intuitive only after enough exposure to real narrated Russian rather than through rule-memorization alone.
title: Unidirectional vs multidirectional pairs
explanation: идти (one direction, now) vs ходить (repeatedly/around/there-and-back); ехать vs ездить (by vehicle).

examples.gloss: I'm on my way to the movies (right now, one direction).

examples.native: Я хожу в кино каждую неделю
examples.gloss: I go to the movies every week. (habitual — multidirectional ходить)
We went to the movies yesterday. (there and back — the round trip is complete)

bridge_note: Russian grammaticalized a directionality distinction English leaves to context.
mistake: the signature error — confusing pair members; идти for habitual motion.
branch: Verbs of Motion

title: Foot vs vehicle distinction
explanation: The unidirectional/multidirectional split just learned for идти/ходить applies again, independently, to a whole family of motion verbs distinguished by *how* the motion happens: идти/ходить for on-foot motion, ехать/ездить for motion by vehicle, and parallel pairs for carrying (нести/носить), leading/guiding (вести/водить), flying (лететь/летать), and swimming (плыть/плавать). Each pair still makes its own separate one-direction-now vs. habitual/repeated distinction on top of the manner distinction, so choosing the right motion verb in Russian actually means answering two independent questions at once — how is the subject moving, and is this a single directed trip or not — where English "go" collapses both into one all-purpose verb.

examples.gloss: I'm going/driving to Moscow. (not иду — that would imply on foot)

bridge_note: English "go" is manner-neutral and works identically whether you're walking or driving ("I'm going to Moscow" says nothing about how), so an English speaker has to learn to encode a piece of information — mode of travel — that English simply never forces into the verb itself, on top of the directionality distinction already learned for идти/ходить.
mistake: using идти/ходить for travel that obviously requires a vehicle, such as going to another city (Я иду в Москву instead of Я еду в Москву), by defaulting to the most familiar motion verb regardless of manner.
branch: Verbs of Motion

title: Prefixed motion verbs (по-, при-, у-, в-, вы-, пере-, до-, за-, под-, от-)
explanation: Prefixes add spatial meaning and aspect: по- makes a perfective "set off" (пойти, поехать); при-/у- = arrive/leave; в-/вы- = enter/exit. The multidirectional stem becomes imperfective, the unidirectional becomes perfective (приходить/прийти).

examples.gloss: He arrived home. (при- + the unidirectional stem идти, now perfective)
She left/drove away. (у- + the unidirectional stem ехать, now perfective)

bridge_note: a spatial prefix bounds the motion, making it perfective, which then needs a re-derived imperfective.
mistake: mismatching aspect stems.
branch: Verbs of Motion

title: Figurative/idiomatic motion verbs
explanation: Once идти's literal "go on foot, one direction, now" sense is solid, it turns out to have a whole second life as a fixed idiom-generating verb applied to things that don't walk at all: время идёт ("time goes by/passes"), дождь идёт (literally "rain walks", i.e. "it's raining"), речь идёт о ("the matter/discussion concerns..."). These aren't productive extensions a learner can generate freely by reasoning about idти's core meaning — they're a closed set of fixed collocations that have to be learned individually as vocabulary, the same way an English learner has to memorize that "time flies" uses "flies" rather than deriving it from how birds move.

examples.gloss: Time goes by / passes. It's raining. (literally: "rain goes/walks")

bridge_note: English does exactly the same kind of thing with its own motion verbs ("time flies", "business is going well"), so the phenomenon of a literal motion verb drifting into abstract idiom isn't foreign — what's unfamiliar is simply which specific idioms Russian happened to build this way, since they don't line up with English's own set at all.
mistake: reading these idioms over-literally as if they described actual walking (imagining rain literally walking); trying to apply the idti/khodit' directionality distinction to these fixed idioms, which don't follow the regular motion-verb rules at all.
branch: Verbs of Motion

long_form:
один behaves like an ordinary agreeing adjective; 2, 3, and 4 force the following noun into genitive singular; 5 and everything above force genitive plural. From an English perspective this looks like one uniform category — "a number followed by a noun" — getting arbitrarily split three ways for no obvious reason, but the three-way split is a direct fossil of real grammatical history, not an arbitrary curriculum choice.

Proto-Indo-European, and early Slavic after it, distinguished not just singular and plural but also a dual number, reserved for exactly two of something. When the dual died out as a living category in the Slavic branch, its old endings for "two" got reinterpreted by later speakers as a distinctive genitive-singular-shaped form of agreement, and три/четыре — which had historically taken the old plural, itself formally similar to genitive singular in the relevant noun classes — rode along with the same reanalysis. Five and above, by contrast, were originally ordinary nouns in their own right (something closer to "a fiver," "a tenner"), which is exactly why they still govern genitive plural today the same way any quantity noun does (стакан воды, "a glass of water") — the boundary between 4 and 5 is a genuine seam in Indo-European grammatical history, preserved almost by accident into the modern counting system.

English numerals never touch noun morphology this way at all: "one table," "two tables," "five tables" flip the noun only once, at the single universal switch between singular and plural. Russian instead runs at least three distinct switches, and adds a wrinkle English has no equivalent for — the numeral два itself carries gender agreement (два stola/okna for masculine and neuter, две books for feminine), a distinction три and четыре don't share at all.

The two reliable English-speaker mistakes are keeping the noun in nominative plural after any number out of habit (importing the English "just pluralize it" reflex wholesale), and, once that's corrected, over-applying genitive singular past the 4-to-5 boundary instead of switching to genitive plural. A third, subtler slip is simply forgetting that два needs its own gender agreement where три/четыре don't.

The system gets genuinely intricate once compound numbers enter the picture: the case-government rule keys off only the very last digit of the whole number, regardless of the number's overall size — двадцать один стол follows the один-rule, двадцать два стола the 2–4 rule, двадцать пять столов the 5+ rule. The logic stays perfectly internally consistent, but the results look wildly inconsistent to anyone who instinctively expects the number's magnitude, rather than its last digit, to matter.
title: Cardinal 1–10 and the counting-case rule
explanation: 1 agrees like an adjective (один стол, одна книга); 2, 3, 4 → genitive singular (два стола, три книги); 5+ → genitive plural (пять столов). Unlike 3 and 4, the numeral 2 itself has a separate feminine form (два for m/n, две for f) that must agree with the noun's gender — две книги but два стола/окна.

examples.native: одна минута, две минуты, пять минут
examples.gloss: one minute; two minutes; five minutes (1 agrees like an adjective, 2–4 take genitive singular, 5+ take genitive plural)

bridge_note: 2 historically took the dual (now lost), 3–4 a plural merged with the genitive singular; 5+ were nouns ("a fiver of tables") governing the genitive plural — the 4-vs-5 "barrier".
mistake: nominative plural after 2–4 (the English instinct); genitive singular after 5+; forgetting 2 has a feminine form (две), unlike 3/4 which don't change for gender.
branch: Numerals and Quantity

title: Compound numerals and the "last digit" rule
explanation: When a number is written out as more than one word, the noun's case-agreement rule is determined entirely by the very last word of the number, with the rest of the number completely irrelevant to the calculation — двадцать один стол follows the один-rule (agreeing like an adjective) purely because один is the last word, even though the overall quantity is twenty-one, and двадцать два стола follows the 2–4 rule for the same reason. This produces results that look wildly inconsistent to someone expecting the number's *size* to matter (a bigger number "should" behave differently from a small one), when the actual governing principle — check only the last digit — is perfectly regular once separated from that intuition.

examples.gloss: thirty-one books (lit. "thirty [and] one book" — the noun's case follows один, the 1-rule, even though the whole number is over thirty)

bridge_note: English pluralization keys off the number's overall size in a sense that never revisits the last digit specifically — "twenty-one tables", "twenty-two tables", and "one hundred tables" all just take the plural "tables" regardless of the final digit — so there's no English habit of re-checking a compound number's very last word before deciding the noun's form.
mistake: keying the noun's case off the number's overall magnitude instead of its last word (assuming any number over twenty needs the genitive-plural treatment 5+ numbers require); forgetting that a compound ending in один still triggers singular adjective-like agreement no matter how large the whole number is.
branch: Numerals and Quantity

title: Ordinal numerals
explanation: Ordinals (первый, второй, пятый — "first, second, fifth") are grammatically ordinary long-form adjectives, agreeing in gender/number/case with whatever they modify exactly like новый does, which makes them far more regular to handle than cardinal numerals (previous point), whose case-agreement rules are genuinely irregular. Dates exploit this directly: a date is expressed as a neuter ordinal agreeing with the implicit word число ("date/number"), so первое января ("the first of January") uses the neuter ordinal form and января stays genitive ("of January") regardless of which ordinal or which month is named.

examples.native: первое января, в две тысячи двадцатом году
examples.gloss: the first of January; in the year 2020 (ordinals decline like adjectives)

bridge_note: English ordinals ("first", "second") are just as invariant as English cardinals and never agree with anything, and English dates use the ordinal without touching the month's form ("the first of January") — so an English speaker has no built-in reflex either to decline первое or to expect января to sit in the genitive rather than some form matching первое.
mistake: leaving ordinals undeclined the way English ones are; using a cardinal number instead of the required ordinal when stating a date (saying один instead of первое for "the first").
branch: Numerals and Quantity

title: Declension of cardinal numerals
explanation: Once a cardinal numeral is used in any case besides nominative/accusative, the numeral itself has to decline, on top of whatever case-agreement effect it's already imposing on its noun — пять becomes пяти (genitive/dative/prepositional) or пятью (instrumental), each a distinct form to memorize rather than a predictable extension of the nominative. Compound numbers make this considerably harder because every word in the compound declines independently and simultaneously (двести declines its "two" component and its "hundred" component separately, not as one fused unit), which is exactly why Wade and other reference grammars single numeral declension out as one of the genuinely hardest corners of Russian morphology.

examples.native: с пятью рублями; о двухстах студентах
examples.gloss: with five rubles; about two hundred students (the numeral itself takes the case here, not just the noun)

bridge_note: English numbers never change form no matter what role they play in the sentence ("with five rubles", "about two hundred students" both keep "five" and "two hundred" completely unchanged) — so this is one of the few points in the whole curriculum where an English speaker isn't just applying a familiar mechanism (agreement, case-marking) to new vocabulary, but learning that numbers themselves are full-fledged declinable words in Russian, a category English numbers simply aren't.
mistake: leaving numerals undeclined in oblique cases out of habit from English (с пять рублями instead of с пятью рублями); declining only one part of a compound number and leaving the rest in the nominative.
source: Wade flags numeral declension as a notorious problem area.
branch: Numerals and Quantity

title: Collective numerals (двое, трое, четверо)
explanation: Alongside the ordinary cardinal numbers, Russian has a separate small set of collective numerals (двое, трое, четверо, and a few higher ones with declining frequency) reserved for specific noun categories rather than for counting in general: groups of people referred to together, groups explicitly of males, nouns that only exist in plural form (pluralia tantum, like сутки "a 24-hour period"), and children/young of any kind (дети, ребята). Their existence reflects an older layer of the numeral system that survived only in these narrow lexical pockets rather than generalizing across all nouns, which is why двое детей sounds natural while a plain feminine noun like *двое женщин is not — collective numerals are specifically incompatible with feminine nouns.

examples.gloss: two children; three days/nights (used with groups of people and pluralia-tantum nouns like сутки)

bridge_note: English has no equivalent second numeral system at all — "two" counts everything regardless of what kind of noun follows it — so an English speaker has to accept that a completely separate, narrower-use counting word set exists in Russian for specific noun classes, something with no partial analogue to lean on.
mistake: using a collective numeral with a feminine noun, where only the plain cardinal is grammatical; over-using collective numerals as a stylistic "more natural-sounding" choice when the ordinary cardinal is actually the correct, unmarked option for most nouns.
branch: Numerals and Quantity

title: Time, age, dates, quantity words
explanation: This point ties together several already-learned pieces into their most common real-world uses: age is stated with the person in dative and no verb at all (Мне двадцать лет, lit. "to me [there are] twenty years", following the same experiencer-dative logic as necessity in Unit 5), and indefinite quantity words (много "a lot", мало "few", несколько "several") govern the genitive plural of whatever they quantify, the same case a specific number 5+ would require. Telling time also plugs into the numeral system already covered — Сейчас два часа applies the same 1/2–4/5+ agreement rule to the word час ("o'clock/hour") that any other counted noun would follow.

examples.gloss: It's two o'clock now.

bridge_note: English states age with a subject and "to be" ("I am twenty"), giving no hint that Russian instead treats age as something that happens to a dative experiencer with no nominative subject at all — the same structural mismatch already seen with necessity and dative-experiencer verbs, now recurring in yet another everyday context.
mistake: using nominative after quantity words (много книга instead of много книг) instead of the required genitive plural; stating age with a nominative subject and a verb, importing the English "I am twenty" structure directly.
branch: Numerals and Quantity

long_form:
A participle takes a verb — keeping its aspect, its tense reference, and its case/preposition government intact — and dresses it in adjective clothing, letting it agree in gender, number, and case with whatever noun it modifies. Russian builds four of them along two independent axes, active/passive crossed with present/past, so a single relative-clause idea (the student who reads / who read / being read about / that was read) folds into one agreeing word instead of a full separate clause.

Participles are an ancient, inherited Indo-European verbal category — Latin and Greek both carry rich participle systems of their own — and Russian's held onto them with unusual tenacity in its written register even as ordinary spoken Russian drifted toward preferring который-clauses for the exact same job. That split hardened historically as literary Russian standardized partly under the influence of Church Slavonic, which retained participles (and their close cousins, gerunds/deepричастия) as a hallmark of elevated, bookish style, while colloquial speech simplified toward the more analytic, который-based alternative that feels natural in conversation.

English participles (reading, read, having read) exist but are far more restricted in what they can do. English can say "the reading student" for a narrow set of adjective-like participles, but it can't agree a participle with case the way Russian does, and it can't productively build a full phrase with its own dependent objects and adverbs compressed into a single agreeing word the way a Russian причастный оборот can. English relies on relative clauses ("the student who is reading") to do almost all of the work Russian participles compress into one word instead.

The most common structural mistake isn't a grammatical error so much as a register error: expecting to hear participles in everyday spoken Russian the way they appear constantly in written texts. They're a genuinely bookish marker, and overusing them in casual conversation reads as stilted or pretentious — the reverse of the usual learner problem of underusing a feature rather than reaching for it in the wrong setting.

Each of the four participle types carries its own aspectual restriction worth understanding rather than just memorizing: active present and passive present participles can only form from imperfective verbs, because "in the process of doing X" or "currently being done" presupposes an action still ongoing, with no completed result yet — a restriction that follows directly and logically from what aspect itself means, once aspect (Unit 9) is already understood. The whole participle system, in other words, is a natural extension of the aspect system already learned, not a separate new set of arbitrary facts layered on top.
title: The concept of the participle (причастие)
explanation: A verb form behaving like an adjective, agreeing in gender/number/case while keeping the verb's aspect and government. Four types: active present, active past, passive present, passive past.

examples.gloss: reading (active present), who read (active past), being read (passive present), having been read (passive past)

bridge_note: participles are the written language's compression device — a whole который-clause folded into one agreeing word; everyday speech prefers который instead.
mistake: expecting them in speech (they are bookish).
source: Std B1: "Понятие о причастии"; B2: "Причастие, причастный оборот"
branch: Participles and Gerunds (Verbal Adverbs)

title: Active present participle (-ущ-/-ющ-/-ащ-/-ящ-)
explanation: This participle compresses "the one who is currently doing X" into a single agreeing adjective-like word, built by taking a verb's third-person-plural present-tense form, stripping its personal ending, and adding -щ- plus adjective agreement endings (читают → читающий, "the one reading"). Because it names an action still in progress with no completed result, it can only be formed from imperfective verbs — a perfective verb has no ongoing present-tense meaning for the participle to express (Unit 9's perfective-future logic applies here too), so "the one who will read" simply has no active-present-participle equivalent at all.

examples.gloss: the student who is reading (lit. "the reading student")

bridge_note: English "-ing" participles ("the reading student") look like a direct match, but English "-ing" freely combines with any verb regardless of a category Russian aspect enforces strictly — English speakers have no built-in check for whether a verb "is allowed" to form this kind of participle, since in English it always is.
mistake: trying to form an active present participle from a perfective verb (grammatically impossible, not just unusual); using this bookish written form in casual conversation, where который is the natural spoken equivalent.
branch: Participles and Gerunds (Verbal Adverbs)

title: Active past participle (-вш-/-ш-)
explanation: This participle compresses "the one who did/was doing X" into one agreeing word, built from the past-tense (the -л form's) stem by replacing -л with -вш- (or just -ш- after a consonant): читал→читавший, сдал→сдавший. Unlike the active present participle, it can be built from either aspect, because past reference alone is compatible with both an ongoing past action (imperfective) and a single completed one (perfective) — the aspect distinction it inherits from its source verb still carries the same imperfective/perfective meaning difference the finite past tense would have had.

examples.gloss: the student who passed the exam

bridge_note: English "having done" and simple "-ed" participles ("the student who passed") don't carry a grammaticalized aspect choice the way this participle inherits one from its source verb — an English speaker has no habit of checking whether the underlying action was a completed whole or an ongoing process before choosing the participle form.
mistake: picking the wrong aspect for the intended meaning (using a perfective-based participle where the ongoing, imperfective sense was intended, or vice versa); confusing this participle's -вш-/-ш- with the passive past participle's -нн-/-т- (next point), which look superficially similar but mark a completely different grammatical relationship.
branch: Participles and Gerunds (Verbal Adverbs)

title: Passive present participle (-ем-/-им-)
explanation: This participle compresses "the thing currently being X-ed (by someone)" into one agreeing word, formed by adding -ем-/-им- to the present stem of a transitive verb: изучать→изучаемый ("being studied"). It requires two conditions at once — imperfective aspect, for the same ongoing-action reason the active present participle needs it, and transitivity, because a passive by definition needs an implicit agent doing the action *to* the noun, which only a transitive verb (one that takes a direct object) can supply. It's also the rarest of the four participle types in real usage, largely confined to formal/scientific writing, since spoken Russian almost always prefers the -ся passive construction (Unit 12's passive-voice point) for the same meaning.

examples.gloss: the language being studied

bridge_note: English "being studied" is built compositionally from "be" + a passive participle and works with essentially any transitive verb without a special aspect restriction — Russian's version instead has to satisfy both the aspect restriction already learned for active participles and a transitivity check, stacking two separate conditions an English speaker isn't used to verifying at once.
mistake: trying to form this participle from an intransitive verb, which has no implicit object for the passive meaning to attach to; over-using it in speech, where the -ся passive is the natural everyday choice and this form reads as stiff or bookish.
branch: Participles and Gerunds (Verbal Adverbs)

title: Passive past participle (-нн-/-енн-/-т-) — long and short
explanation: "Having been X-ed"; the short form is very common as a predicate and forms the passive. Examples (long): прочитанная книга; (short): Книга прочитана. Дом построен в 1990 году.

examples.gloss: the book that was read (long form) / The book is read. (short-form predicate)

bridge_note: short passive participle + (был/будет) is the normal analytic passive for perfective verbs.
mistake: -н-/-нн- spelling; leaving the short form unagreed.
branch: Participles and Gerunds (Verbal Adverbs)

title: The passive voice and active↔passive transformation
explanation: Russian splits the passive voice by aspect rather than using one uniform construction the way English "is/was done" does: an ongoing or repeated passive process uses the -ся passive built on an imperfective verb (Дом строится, "the house is being built"), while a completed passive result uses the short-form past passive participle from Unit 12, built on a perfective verb (Дом построен, "the house is/was built"). In both constructions, the agent — if named at all — goes into the instrumental case rather than a prepositional phrase (построен рабочими, "built by workers"), continuing the instrumental's core "means/agency" function from Unit 5 rather than introducing a new preposition-based "by"-phrase the way English does.

examples.gloss: The city was founded by Peter the Great. (the agent, Петром Первым, is instrumental)

bridge_note: English marks its passive agent with the preposition "by" regardless of aspect or tense ("is built by", "was built by"), giving no signal that Russian instead (a) splits the whole passive construction by aspect and (b) marks the agent with a bare case ending rather than any preposition at all.
mistake: putting the agent in a prepositional phrase or the nominative instead of the instrumental, importing English "by"; picking the wrong passive construction for the verb's aspect (using -ся for a completed result, or the short participle for an ongoing process).
source: B2 Std §2.3.7: "Правила трансформации действительных и страдательных конструкций"
branch: Participles and Gerunds (Verbal Adverbs)

title: The gerund/verbal adverb (деепричастие)
explanation: The gerund compresses a whole adverbial clause ("while doing X" or "having done X") into a single indeclinable word attached to the main clause's verb — indeclinable because, unlike a participle, it modifies the action itself rather than agreeing with any noun. Its aspect encodes its timing relative to the main verb: an imperfective gerund (-я/-а) marks an action simultaneous with the main verb (Читая, он улыбался, "While reading, he smiled"), while a perfective gerund (-в/-вши) marks an action that happened before the main verb (Прочитав письмо, она заплакала, "Having read the letter, she cried"). The one non-negotiable rule governing every gerund is that it must share its subject with the main verb — there is no independent subject slot for the gerund's action at all.

examples.gloss: Having looked left, Sergei crossed the street. (perfective gerund -в: the action happens before the main verb, same subject throughout)

bridge_note: English "-ing" clauses ("having read the letter, she cried") permit exactly the same shared-subject requirement in careful writing — English style guides call violating it a "dangling modifier" — but English usage is far more tolerant of dangling constructions in casual speech than Russian is of a dangling деепричастие, which reads as a flagged, recognized error rather than a minor stylistic lapse.
mistake: the classic dangling error, giving the gerund's implied subject a different referent than the main clause's subject (Подъезжая к станции, у меня слетела шляпа is famously wrong because "approaching the station" has no grammatical subject in the main clause for it to share); confusing which gerund suffix marks simultaneous vs. prior action.
branch: Participles and Gerunds (Verbal Adverbs)

title: Transforming participial/gerund phrases ↔ clauses
explanation: This point is the practical payoff of understanding participles and gerunds as *compressions* of ordinary clauses rather than as separate grammar to memorize in isolation: because a причастный оборот (participial phrase) is functionally equivalent to a который-clause, and a деепричастный оборот (gerund phrase) is functionally equivalent to an adverbial time/manner clause, either can be mechanically expanded into the other. Студент, сдавший экзамен expands to Студент, который сдал экзамен with no change in meaning, just a shift in register from compressed/written to explicit/spoken; the skill being tested is converting fluently in both directions while keeping the aspect and tense of the underlying verb intact through the transformation.

examples.native: Студент, сдавший экзамен ↔ Студент, который сдал экзамен.
examples.gloss: The student who passed the exam (participle phrase ↔ который-clause, same meaning)

bridge_note: English can also compress a relative clause into a participial phrase ("the student who passed" / "the student having passed"), so the underlying idea of two equivalent structures is familiar — what's unfamiliar is that Russian expects fluent two-way conversion as a tested B2/C1 skill, where English speakers use participial compression only occasionally and never practice converting it back out explicitly.
mistake: comma errors around the participial or gerund phrase when converting it into a full clause; aspect drift, where the который-clause's verb ends up in a different aspect than the participle it was converted from, subtly changing the meaning.
branch: Participles and Gerunds (Verbal Adverbs)

title: Subordinating conjunctions (cause, time, concession, result)
explanation: Russian has a dedicated conjunction (or small family of near-synonymous conjunctions) for each major logical relationship between clauses: cause (потому что/так как), time (когда/пока/после того как/прежде чем), concession (хотя/несмотря на то что), and result (поэтому/так что). Several of these are themselves compound phrases built from a preposition plus то ("that") plus что/как (после того как literally "after that how/that"), which is why they look bulkier than their English one-word translations — the B2-level additions (благодаря тому что "thanks to the fact that", из-за того что "because of the fact that", по мере того как "to the extent that") follow the exact same compound pattern, just built on more specialized prepositions.

examples.native: Я остался дома, потому что шёл дождь
examples.gloss: I stayed home because it was raining.

bridge_note: English also builds some subordinators out of multiple words ("in spite of the fact that", "as long as"), so the compound-phrase pattern itself is familiar — the difference is how much more systematically Russian does it, turning what English treats as a handful of idiomatic exceptions into the regular, productive way most subordinators above the A1 core are built.
mistake: comma placement around subordinate clauses, since Russian punctuation rules for subordination are stricter and more consistently applied than English's; mixing что ("that", stating a fact) and чтобы ("so that/in order to", purpose) since both can loosely translate as "that" in English.
source: B1 vs B2 conjunction inventories per the State Standard.
branch: Complex Sentences, Mood, and Reported Speech

title: что vs чтобы
explanation: что and чтобы both loosely translate as English "that", but they mark two entirely different relationships between clauses and are never interchangeable: что introduces a factual, indicative statement of what is or was the case (Я знаю, что он здесь, "I know that he's here" — a plain fact), while чтобы introduces purpose or desire and forces the following verb into either the infinitive or the past-tense-plus-irrealis form, never a plain present/future indicative (Я хочу, чтобы он пришёл — literally "I want that he would come"). The verb governing the clause decides which is required: verbs of knowing/saying/perceiving take что because they report facts, while verbs of wanting/requesting take чтобы because they express an unrealized goal rather than a fact.

examples.gloss: I know (that) he's here.
I want him to come. (lit. "that he would come" — чтобы forces the irrealis past-form verb)

bridge_note: English "that" covers both jobs with a single unchanging word ("I know that he's here" / "I want that he comes" — though English actually prefers an infinitive here, "I want him to come"), so there's no surface signal in English pushing a learner to expect two grammatically distinct Russian words; чтобы is literally что + бы, carrying the same irrealis particle used in the conditional mood (Unit 13's next point), which is why it always demands a past-form or infinitive verb rather than an ordinary present/future.
mistake: using что after verbs of wishing/requesting where чтобы is grammatically required (Я хочу, что он пришёл is simply wrong, not just awkward); forgetting that чтобы forces the past-tense-plus-irrealis form on its verb rather than a normal present/future.
branch: Complex Sentences, Mood, and Reported Speech

long_form:
Russian builds every hypothetical, counterfactual, and polite-wish meaning out of a single recipe: a past-tense verb form plus the small, invariable particle бы, which never conjugates, never wanders far from its verb, and single-handedly carries the modal weight that English spreads across a whole family of distinct auxiliaries — would, could, might, should.

бы is a fossil of the old aorist form of быть, a simple past tense Common Slavic once maintained (alongside a parallel imperfect past) before those older tenses collapsed into the single unified past tense Russian uses today. When the old tense system died out, this one leftover fragment of быть's aorist survived — drained entirely of its original meaning "was" — and got reanalyzed by later speakers as a free-floating particle that could attach to any verb to signal irrealis mood instead. It's a striking case of an entire inflected verb form outliving its own paradigm by centuries, surviving only as a one-syllable particle long after the tense system that produced it had vanished.

English, by contrast, built a rich, semantically differentiated set of modal verbs, each carrying its own distinct flavor of hypothetical, ability, permission, or obligation, each with its own (often irregular) conjugation history. Russian collapses all of that distinction-making into one uniform strategy — past tense plus бы — and leaves context, along with the surrounding clause (если бы for unreal conditions, чтобы after verbs of wanting), to carry the finer shades of meaning that English pushes onto the choice of modal verb itself. Which means an English speaker has to consciously unlearn the instinct to go hunting for a different Russian "word" corresponding to each of would, could, might, and should.

The two persistent mistakes both come from treating бы like something it isn't: trying to conjugate it as though it were a normal auxiliary verb, adding person or number agreement it can never take, and separately, importing English tense logic into если-clauses by reaching for a future-tense verb after если бы instead of the required past-tense-plus-бы pattern in both the if-clause and the main clause.

A nuance worth knowing: бы doesn't have to sit next to a sentence's main verb at all — it routinely fuses directly onto a conjunction to form what's effectively a single word (чтобы, хотя бы), which is exactly why бы keeps reappearing scattered across several unrelated-looking topics in this curriculum (что vs. чтобы, unreal conditionals) rather than living tidily inside one "conditional mood" section. It's genuinely one particle doing real structural work across multiple, only loosely related constructions.
title: The conditional/subjunctive mood with бы
explanation: Past-tense verb + invariable бы = hypothetical/counterfactual and polite wishes; real conditions use если + future, unreal use если бы + past + past+бы.

examples.gloss: I would like… (polite wish)

examples.native: Если бы я знал, я бы сказал
examples.gloss: If I had known, I would have said (so). (unreal conditional: если бы + past, main clause + past + бы)

bridge_note: Russian has no morphological conditional — it recycles the past tense plus the invariable particle бы (a reduced old aorist of быть).
mistake: conjugating a special conditional; future after если бы.
source: B2 Std names сослагательное наклонение and adds бы to the particle set.
branch: Complex Sentences, Mood, and Reported Speech

title: Reported (indirect) speech
explanation: Russian reports speech by keeping the tense the original speaker actually used, rather than shifting it backward the way English does — the reporting is anchored to the original moment of speech, not recalculated relative to the moment of reporting. Which conjunction introduces the reported clause depends on what kind of original utterance is being reported: a statement becomes что + the original tense, a command becomes чтобы + a past-form verb (matching чтобы's general irrealis requirement), and a question becomes ли (for yes/no questions) or the original question word (for wh-questions) followed by the original tense, with word order shifting to statement order.

examples.gloss: lit. "he said that he will come"
She asked whether I would come. (ли marks a reported yes/no question)

bridge_note: Russian reports from the original speaker's vantage point — there's no sequence-of-tenses shift the way English backshifts "will" to "would".
mistake: importing English backshift — turning придёт ("will come") into a past-tense form when reporting it later, the way English shifts "will" to "would"; using что for a reported command or question instead of чтобы/ли, since English "that" can superficially cover all three.
source: B1 §2.3.4: "Правила перевода прямой речи в косвенную"
branch: Complex Sentences, Mood, and Reported Speech

title: Neutral SVO and why order is "free but not random"
explanation: Russian's unmarked, out-of-context word order is subject-verb-object, the same as English — so a beginner can produce and understand basic sentences using only SVO and never notice case is doing anything word-order couldn't already do. What changes once case is fully internalized is that SVO stops being the *only* grammatical order: because the endings already mark who did what to whom, every one of the six possible orderings of subject/verb/object remains fully grammatical, with the choice among them driven by what information is being emphasized (Unit 14's next point) rather than by syntax breaking down.

examples.gloss: The student is reading a book. (neutral SVO — though case endings would allow any word order)

bridge_note: English SVO order is not optional the way Russian's is — it's the only mechanism English has left for marking grammatical roles at all, so reordering an English sentence genuinely changes who did what to whom. Reordering a Russian sentence, by contrast, leaves the roles exactly as the endings marked them; it only shifts emphasis, which is a fundamentally different kind of "changing the sentence" than an English speaker's instincts predict.
mistake: assuming a reordered Russian sentence must mean something different grammatically, the way it would in English, rather than recognizing it as the same roles with different emphasis; conversely, relying on word order rather than endings to figure out who did what when reading non-SVO Russian.
branch: Word Order, Information Structure, and Register

long_form:
Because case endings already mark grammatical roles, Russian word order is freed up to do a completely different job: signaling what's already known in the conversation (тема, theme) versus what's new or important (рема, rheme). The rule of thumb is that the rheme — carrying the main informational payload, usually also the strongest sentence stress — goes last, so На столе книги ("what's on the table is books") and Книги на столе ("where the books are is on the table") are both perfectly grammatical, differing only in which piece of information the sentence is actually delivering.

This is the domain linguists call functional sentence perspective, most closely associated with the Prague School and Vilém Mathesius, who observed that languages with rich case systems and no articles tend to grammaticalize information structure through word order precisely because they can afford to move constituents around freely without breaking who-did-what-to-whom — that job is already handled by the endings. Russian is close to a textbook case of this typological trade-off, alongside other richly inflected, article-less languages that make the same move.

English has no case system flexible enough to permit this kind of reordering, but it isn't blind to the same communicative need — it just pays for it differently. Definite and indefinite articles do a large part of the job ("a book" signaling new information, "the book" signaling given information), sentence stress does more, and a smaller menu of syntactic tools — passive voice, cleft sentences like "it was books that were on the table" — covers what's left. Russian and English are solving the same problem with different currencies: Russian pays with morphology and word-order freedom, English pays with a determiner system Russian doesn't have at all.

The reliable English-speaker mistake is front-loading new information out of habit, since English so often fronts or stresses the element being introduced — producing a Russian sentence that's fully grammatical but subtly backwards in emphasis, understandable but distinctly foreign-sounding in a way no case ending ever would be.

Worth noting: this is exactly the gap no article system fills in Russian. A bare noun like книга carries no built-in marker distinguishing "a book" from "the book" the way English articles would, so word order (and, in speech, intonation) ends up doing double duty — carrying both the definiteness signal and the theme-rheme signal that English splits between articles and stress. That double duty is precisely why mastering Russian word order at a genuinely native level is treated as a B2/C1 skill rather than a beginner one, even though the underlying rule — new information last — sounds almost trivially simple stated in a single sentence.
title: Theme–rheme / given–new: the focus goes last
explanation: Known info (тема) first; new/important info (рема) last, carrying logical stress.

examples.gloss: "what's on the table is books"
"where the books are is the table"

bridge_note: with no articles, Russian leans on word order to do what English does with "a"/"the" and sentence stress — old information first, new information last.
mistake: front-loading new info as in English.
source: Prague-school/functional-sentence-perspective analysis; exact CEFR level is a judgment call.
branch: Word Order, Information Structure, and Register

title: Focus/emphatic particles (же, ведь, -то, даже, именно, только)
explanation: This closed set of small, unstressed words adds a layer of emphasis or attitude on top of a sentence's plain content without changing its basic meaning — each particle attaches to (and takes scope over) whatever word immediately follows or precedes it, so its placement is what determines what's being emphasized. же adds impatience or a "reminder" tone (Я же говорил!, "I told you [so]!"); ведь appeals to shared/obvious knowledge; -то attaches directly onto a word as a suffix to mark it as topical or slightly vague; даже means "even"; именно singles something out precisely ("exactly/specifically"); только restricts to "only". Because none of these have a clean one-word English translation, they're usually rendered by English sentence stress or an inserted phrase instead of a matching particle, which is exactly why omitting them makes Russian sound flatter than intended.

examples.native: Я же говорил! Именно он это сделал
examples.gloss: I told you so! (же adds emphasis/reminder) It was exactly him who did it. (именно singles out он)

bridge_note: English carries most of this same emphatic/attitudinal information through pitch and stress alone ("I DID tell you", spoken with heavy stress on "did") rather than through a dedicated word, so an English speaker's instinct in writing is to leave the emphasis unmarked entirely — Russian instead lexicalizes much of that stress-based meaning into small words that have to be actively inserted, not just implied by tone of voice.
mistake: omitting these particles entirely, producing grammatically correct but emotionally flat sentences that miss the intended emphasis or attitude; misplacing a particle relative to the word it should be scoping over, which shifts what's being emphasized.
branch: Word Order, Information Structure, and Register

title: Negation scope with не
explanation: не doesn't attach to the verb by default the way English "not" does — it attaches directly to whichever specific word is being negated, and that word can be the verb, the subject, or the object depending on what the speaker actually means to deny. Я не читаю книгу denies the reading itself; Не я читаю книгу denies that "I" am the one doing the reading (someone else is); Я читаю не книгу denies that a book is the thing being read (it's something else). Because не's position is what carries the meaning, moving it is not a stylistic choice but a genuine change in what's being negated — the same sentence with не in three different spots makes three different claims.

examples.native: Я не читаю книгу / Не я читаю книгу / Я читаю не книгу
examples.gloss: I'm not reading a book. / It's not me who's reading a book. / It's not a book that I'm reading. (не shifts right before whatever it negates)

bridge_note: English negation attaches to the auxiliary/verb almost universally, and to isolate "it wasn't me who read the book" or "it wasn't a book that I read" English has to reach for a whole cleft-sentence construction — Russian achieves the same narrow, targeted negation just by relocating one small word, with no extra sentence machinery needed.
mistake: always placing не directly before the verb regardless of what's actually being negated, the fixed pattern English negation trains; missing that a genuinely different meaning is available (and required) by moving не to scope over the subject or object instead.
branch: Word Order, Information Structure, and Register

title: Register: ты vs вы and politeness
explanation: вы does double duty as both the grammatical plural "you" for any group and the polite/formal singular "you" for one person you're not on familiar terms with, while ты is reserved for informal singular address only — family, close friends, children, and, among young people, most peers. This isn't a free stylistic choice: using ты with a stranger, a superior, or an older person you've just met is a real social error in Russian in a way that skipping a courtesy title in English usually isn't, because the choice is obligatory and grammatically forces agreement on the verb (Как вас зовут? vs. Как тебя зовут?) every single time you address someone directly, with no neutral option available.

examples.gloss: What's your name? (formal/plural вы)
What's your name? (informal ты)

bridge_note: вы-politeness is a European convention layered onto the true plural.
mistake: using ты with strangers, superiors, or older people by analogy with English "you", which makes no such distinction at all and gives an English speaker no instinct that this choice even needs to be made; switching to ты too early in a new relationship, which can read as presumptuous even once a learner knows the distinction exists.
branch: Word Order, Information Structure, and Register

title: Functional-stylistic register (colloquial vs neutral vs bookish/official)
explanation: This is the point where every previously separate "bookish" feature of the curriculum — participles, gerunds, the passive voice, compound subordinating conjunctions — gets recognized as belonging to one coherent register rather than being scattered advanced grammar. Formal/scientific/official Russian favors a nominal style (piling up noun phrases and fixed verb-noun collocations, like оказать помощь, "render assistance", instead of the plainer помочь, "help") and reaches for participles and gerunds routinely, while colloquial speech systematically avoids all of that in favor of который-clauses, separate short sentences, and simpler verbs. Genuine command of Russian at B2/C1 means actively choosing between these registers based on context, not just being able to produce grammatical sentences in one of them.

examples.gloss: I hereby inform you... (bookish/official) vs Listen, basically... (colloquial) — same content, different register

bridge_note: English also has a colloquial/formal split (contractions and phrasal verbs vs. Latinate vocabulary and full clauses), so the general idea of register-switching is familiar — the difference is that Russian's formal register recruits entire grammatical categories (participles, gerunds, the passive) that a learner might otherwise think of as just "advanced grammar" rather than as a register marker to deploy or avoid situationally.
mistake: using bookish participles, gerunds, or nominal-style collocations in casual speech, where they read as stilted or pretentious rather than simply "more advanced"; using colloquial vocabulary or overly simple sentence structure in formal writing, where the nominal/participial style is actually expected.
branch: Word Order, Information Structure, and Register
